q: Choose the word closest in meaning to WARY.

q: Choose the word closest in meaning to ENIGMA.

q: Choose the word closest in meaning to GARRULOUS.

q: Choose the word closest in meaning to HAUGHTY.

q: Choose the word closest in meaning to INDIGENOUS.

q: Choose the word closest in meaning to LACONIC.

q: Choose the word closest in meaning to MITIGATE.

q: Choose the word closest in meaning to NOVICE.

q: Choose the word closest in meaning to OBDURATE.

q: Choose the word closest in meaning to PRAGMATIC.

q: Choose the word closest in meaning to REDUNDANT.
e: Redundant means no longer needed.

q: Choose the word closest in meaning to SPURIOUS.
e: Spurious means false though appearing genuine.

q: Choose the word closest in meaning to TENACIOUS.

q: Choose the word closest in meaning to VENERATE.

q: Choose the word closest in meaning to PUSILLANIMOUS.

q: Choose the word closest in meaning to SOBRIQUET.

q: Choose the word closest in meaning to VERISIMILITUDE.
e: Verisimilitude is the quality of seeming real.

q: Choose the word opposite in meaning to SCANTY.

q: Choose the word opposite in meaning to NASCENT.
e: Nascent means just beginning to develop.

q: Choose the word opposite in meaning to ARID.

q: Choose the word opposite in meaning to BENIGN.

q: Choose the word opposite in meaning to CONCEAL.

q: Choose the word opposite in meaning to DILATE.
e: To dilate is to widen.

q: Choose the word opposite in meaning to EXPAND.

q: Choose the word opposite in meaning to FRIVOLOUS.

q: Choose the word opposite in meaning to GENEROUS.
e: A miserly person hates to spend or give.

q: Choose the word opposite in meaning to HOSTILE.
e: Hostile means unfriendly.

q: Choose the word opposite in meaning to INNOCENT.
e: Innocent means not guilty.

q: Choose the word opposite in meaning to JUVENILE.

q: Choose the word opposite in meaning to KNOWLEDGE.

q: Choose the word opposite in meaning to LENIENT.

q: Choose the word opposite in meaning to MODEST.
e: Modest people do not show off.

q: Choose the word opposite in meaning to NOTORIOUS.

q: Choose the word opposite in meaning to OPAQUE.

q: Choose the word opposite in meaning to PERMANENT.

q: Choose the word opposite in meaning to RIGID.

q: Choose the word opposite in meaning to SCARCE.
e: Scarce means in short supply.

q: Choose the word opposite in meaning to TIMID.
e: Timid means easily frightened.

q: Choose the word opposite in meaning to URBAN.
e: Urban relates to towns; rural to the countryside.

q: Choose the word opposite in meaning to VAGUE.
e: Vague means not clear.

q: Choose the word opposite in meaning to WAX (as a verb).
e: The moon waxes (grows) and wanes (shrinks).

q: Choose the word opposite in meaning to ZENITH.

q: Choose the word opposite in meaning to BRAVERY.

q: Choose the word opposite in meaning to EGREGIOUS.

q: Author : Novel :: Composer : ______
e: An author creates a novel; a composer creates a symphony.

e: Each instrument is paired with what it measures.

q: Index : Book :: Legend : ______

e: Each adjective lacks the quality named.

q: Surgeon : Scalpel :: Sculptor : ______
e: Each worker is paired with a tool.

e: Each first item grows into the second.

q: A person who does not believe in the existence of God is:

e: Extempore means spoken without preparation.

e: A polyglot knows several languages.

q: Something that cannot be read is:
e: Illegible writing cannot be read; an illiterate person cannot read.

q: One who walks on foot is:
e: A pedestrian travels on foot.

e: Regicide is the killing of a king.

e: A bibliography lists sources.

e: A panacea is a cure-all.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: Neither of the two answers is correct.
Neither of two answers were correct.
Neither of the two answers are correct.
Neither of the two answer is correct.
e: "Neither" takes a singular verb.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: Each of the boy has a bicycle.
Each of the boys have a bicycle.
Each of the boys has a bicycle.
e: "Each" is singular.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: The committee has submitted its report.
The committee are submitted its report.
The committee have submitted its report.
The committee has submitted their report.
e: A committee acting as one body takes a singular verb and "its".

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: He is one of that men who work hard.
He is one of those men who works hard.
He is one of those man who work hard.
He is one of those men who work hard.
e: "Who" refers to "men", so the verb is plural.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: Walking down the street, the tower came into view.
While walking down the street, a tower appeared.
Walking down the street, a tall tower was seen.
Walking down the street, I saw a tall tower.
e: The opening phrase must describe the subject "I"; the others have dangling modifiers.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: Having finished the work, it was time to go home.
Having finished the work, he went home.
Having finished the work, the home was reached.
Having finished the work, home was where he went.
e: The person who finished the work must be the subject.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: She likes reading, to write and painting.
She likes reading, writing and to paint.
She likes reading, writing and painting.
She likes to read, writing and painting.
e: Items in a list must have the same form (parallel structure).

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: The firm values honesty, working hard and to be punctual.
The firm values honesty, hard work and punctuality.
The firm values honest, hard work and punctuality.
The firm values being honest, hard work and punctual.
e: Three nouns keep the list parallel.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: If I were you, I will accept the offer.
If I am you, I would accept the offer.
If I was you, I will accept the offer.
If I were you, I would accept the offer.
e: An unreal present condition takes "were" and "would".

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: If he had worked hard, he would have passed.
If he has worked hard, he would have passed.
If he worked hard, he would have passed.
If he had worked hard, he would pass.
e: The third conditional uses "had + past participle" and "would have".

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: Hardly he had left when it began to rain.
Hardly had he left than it began to rain.
Hardly had he left when it began to rain.
Hardly did he left when it began to rain.
e: "Hardly" takes inversion and is followed by "when".

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: No sooner had we arrived when the show began.
No sooner we had arrived than the show began.
No sooner did we arrived than the show began.
No sooner had we arrived than the show began.
e: "No sooner" is followed by "than".

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: I wish I am knowing the answer.
I wish I would know the answer.
I wish I knew the answer.
I wish I know the answer.
e: A wish about the present takes the past tense.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: He has been living here for 2015.
He has been living here since 2015.
e: Use the present perfect continuous with "since" and a point of time.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: The news is too good to be true.
The news is too good to true.
The news are too good to be true.
The news were too good to be true.
e: "News" is singular.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
e: Subject names ending in "-ics" take a singular verb.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: Ten kilometres are a long distance to walk.
Ten kilometres were a long distances to walk.
Ten kilometre is a long distance to walk.
Ten kilometres is a long distance to walk.
e: A distance treated as one amount takes a singular verb.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: He gave me a good advice.
He gave me some good advices.
He gave me some good advice.
He gave me many good advices.
e: "Advice" is uncountable.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: She is senior from me by two years.
She is senior to me by two years.
She is more senior than me by two years.
She is senior than me by two years.
e: "Senior", "junior", "superior" and "inferior" take "to".

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: I prefer tea over to coffee.
e: "Prefer" is followed by "to".

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: He is more taller than I am.
He is taller than I am.
He is taller then I am.
He is tallest than I am.
e: Do not use "more" with a comparative ending in "-er".

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: This is the most better of the two books.
This is the best of the two books.
This is best from the two books.
This is the better of the two books.
e: Use the comparative, not the superlative, when comparing two things.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
e: In formal usage "one" is followed by "one's".

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: Between I and you, he is not honest.
Between you and me, he is not honest.
Between you and I, he is not honest.
Among you and me, he is not honest.
e: A preposition takes the object form "me".

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: He asked me where do I live.
He asked me where did I live.
He asked me that where I lived.
He asked me where I lived.
e: An indirect question uses statement word order.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: She told that she was tired.
She said me that she was tired.
She said that she is being tired.
She said that she was tired.
e: "Said" takes no personal object; "told" needs one.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: The teacher said the earth is revolved round the sun.
The teacher said that the earth revolves round the sun.
The teacher said that the earth had revolved round the sun.
The teacher said that the earth revolved round the sun.
e: A universal truth stays in the present tense in reported speech.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: I have known him for ten years.
I am knowing him for ten years.
I know him since ten years.
I have been knowing him since ten years.
e: "Know" is not used in continuous tenses; use "for" with a period.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: When I reached the station, the train has left.
When I had reached the station, the train left.
When I reached the station, the train had left.
When I reached the station, the train left already.
e: The earlier of two past actions takes the past perfect.

q: Choose the correct passive form of "Someone has stolen my watch."
e: Present perfect passive is "has been + past participle".

q: Choose the correct passive form of "They are building a bridge."
e: Present continuous passive is "is being + past participle".

q: Choose the correct indirect form: He said, "I am busy."
o: He said that he is busy now.
He said that I am busy.
He told that he was busy.
He said that he was busy.
e: The pronoun and tense shift in reported speech.

q: Choose the correct indirect form: She said to me, "Do you like tea?"
o: She asked me if I liked tea.
She asked me do I like tea.
She said to me that did I like tea.
She asked me that I liked tea.
e: A yes/no question is reported with "if" or "whether".

q: Fill in the blank: By next June, I ______ here for five years.
e: The future perfect continuous shows duration up to a future point.

q: Fill in the blank: She ______ when the phone rang.
e: The past continuous shows an action in progress in the past.

q: Fill in the blank: The train ______ before we reached the station.
e: The past perfect shows the earlier past action.

q: Fill in the blank: I would rather you ______ at home tonight.
e: "Would rather" + another subject takes the past tense.

q: Fill in the blank: It is high time we ______ the matter.
e: "It is high time" is followed by the past tense.

q: Fill in the blank: He talks as if he ______ everything.
e: "As if" with an unreal sense takes the past tense.

q: Fill in the blank: The labels were photographed ______ their order should be lost.
e: "Lest ... should" means "so that ... not".

q: Fill in the blank: Had I known the truth, I ______ him.
e: "Had I known" is an inverted third conditional.

q: Fill in the blank: Not only ______ late, but he also forgot the file.
e: A sentence starting with "Not only" needs inversion.

q: Fill in the blank: Neither the manager nor the clerks ______ present.
e: With "neither ... nor" the verb agrees with the nearer subject.

q: Fill in the blank: The number of students ______ increasing.
e: "The number of" takes a singular verb; "a number of" takes a plural one.

q: Fill in the blank: A number of books ______ missing from the shelf.
e: "A number of" means "several" and takes a plural verb.

q: Fill in the blank: Bread and butter ______ his usual breakfast.
e: Two nouns forming one idea take a singular verb.

q: Fill in the blank: The manuscript is believed ______ in the tenth century.
e: A passive perfect infinitive is needed for an earlier action done to the subject.

q: Fill in the blank: He is the man ______ I believe can do this job.
e: "Who" is the subject of "can do"; "I believe" is a parenthesis.

q: Fill in the blank: She is the candidate ______ we selected yesterday.
e: "Whom" is the object of "selected".

q: Fill in the blank: He is ______ honest man.
e: "Honest" begins with a vowel sound.

q: Fill in the blank: She studies at ______ university in Lahore.
e: "University" begins with a consonant sound ("yoo").

q: Fill in the blank: ______ Indus is the longest river of Pakistan.
e: Names of rivers take "the".

q: Fill in the blank: ______ sun rises in the east.
e: Unique objects such as the sun and the moon take "the".

q: Fill in the blank: He works hard, ______ he may fail.
e: "Lest" means "for fear that".

q: Fill in the blank: ______ he is poor, he is honest.
e: "Although" introduces a contrast.

q: Fill in the blank: You will not succeed ______ you work hard.
e: "Unless" means "if ... not".

q: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence.
e: The question mark belongs inside the quotation marks.

q: Choose the correct plural.
e: "Criterion" is singular; "criteria" is plural.

q: Choose the correctly spelt word.
e: It has double "c" and double "m".

e: It has double "c", double "r" and ends in "-ence".

q: He is afraid ______ dogs.
e: "Afraid of" is the fixed combination.

q: She is good ______ mathematics.
e: "Good at" a subject or skill.

q: He was accused ______ theft.
e: "Accused of"; compare "charged with".

q: The thief was charged ______ robbery.
e: "Charged with" an offence.

q: I congratulated him ______ his success.
e: "Congratulate on".

q: He died ______ cholera.
e: "Die of" a disease.

q: She is married ______ a doctor.
e: "Married to".

q: He is addicted ______ smoking.
e: "Addicted to".

q: I am not acquainted ______ him.
e: "Acquainted with".

q: The house was sold ______ lieu of unpaid taxes.
e: "In lieu of" means "instead of".

q: His statement is ______ variance with the facts.
e: "At variance with" means "in disagreement with".

q: Her account is consonant ______ the earlier report.
e: "Consonant with" means "in agreement with".

q: This event is anterior ______ the war.
e: "Anterior to" and "posterior to" both take "to".

q: He is devoid ______ common sense.
e: "Devoid of" means "completely lacking".

q: He is well versed ______ Persian literature.
e: "Versed in" means "skilled or experienced in".

q: He is indifferent ______ praise and blame.
e: "Indifferent to".

q: I am tired ______ waiting.
e: "Tired of" means "bored with".

q: He is jealous ______ his brother's success.
e: "Jealous of".

q: Please abide ______ the rules.
e: "Abide by" means "obey".

q: He insisted ______ paying the bill.
e: "Insist on".

q: She succeeded ______ passing the test.
e: "Succeed in".

q: He is confident ______ success.
e: "Confident of".

q: The book is divided ______ five chapters.
e: "Divide into" parts.

q: He was deprived ______ his rights.
e: "Deprived of".

q: She has no control ______ her temper.
e: "Control over".

q: He complied ______ my request.
e: "Comply with".

q: I shall look ______ the matter myself.
e: "Look into" means "investigate".

q: He takes ______ his father.
e: "Take after" means "resemble".

q: The meeting was put ______ till Monday.
e: "Put off" means "postpone".

q: She could not put ______ with the insult.
e: "Put up with" means "tolerate".

q: The plane took ______ at noon.
e: "Take off" means "leave the ground".

q: He has given ______ smoking.
e: "Give up" means "stop doing".

q: The fire brigade put ______ the fire.
e: "Put out" means "extinguish".

q: I came ______ an old friend in the market.
e: "Come across" means "meet by chance".

q: The rebels finally gave ______ .
e: "Give in" means "surrender".

q: "To beat about the bush" means:
e: The speaker talks round the subject.

e: It costs more to keep than it is worth.

q: "To burn the midnight oil" means:

e: It refers to studying or working late.

q: "A bolt from the blue" means:
e: It comes without warning.

q: "To let the cat out of the bag" means:
e: The secret gets out.

q: "At the eleventh hour" means:

q: "To turn a deaf ear" means:

q: "Once in a blue moon" means:

q: "To bury the hatchet" means:

q: "A red-letter day" is:

q: "To smell a rat" means:

e: The person senses trickery.

q: "To hit the nail on the head" means:

e: The remark is exactly right.

q: "To make both ends meet" means:
e: It refers to managing on a small income.

q: "A wild goose chase" is:
e: The search cannot succeed.

q: "To cry over spilt milk" means:
o: To regret what cannot be undone
e: Regret will not change the past.

q: "In black and white" means:
e: The matter is recorded in writing.

q: "To leave no stone unturned" means:
e: Every effort is made.

q: "To see eye to eye" means:
e: The two people share the same view.

q: "To blow one's own trumpet" means:
e: The person boasts.

q: "A fish out of water" is a person who is:
e: The person feels out of place.

q: "To call a spade a spade" means:
e: The speaker is blunt and honest.

q: "To throw in the towel" means:
e: The phrase comes from boxing.

q: "The lion's share" means:
e: One party takes most of something.

q: "To keep one's powder dry" means:
e: It means to remain prepared.

q: "To beard the lion in his den" means:
o: To confront someone powerful on his own ground
e: It is a bold challenge to a powerful person.

q: "To strain at a gnat and swallow a camel" means:
o: To fuss over small faults and ignore big ones
e: It describes misplaced strictness.

q: "To break a butterfly on a wheel" means:
o: To use far too much force for a small matter
To spoil something beautiful by accident
e: Great effort is spent on something trivial.

q: "Forty winks" means:
e: It is a brief nap.

q: "To rest on one's laurels" means:
o: To be satisfied with past success and stop trying
e: The person relies on old achievements.

q: "A Herculean task" is:
o: A task needing great strength or effort
e: It refers to the labours of Hercules.

q: "To read between the lines" means:
e: The reader grasps what is implied.

q: "By hook or by crook" means:
o: By any means, fair or foul
e: Any method will be used.

q: "To be at sixes and sevens" means:
e: Things are in disorder.

q: "A snake in the grass" is:
e: The person pretends to be a friend.

q: "To nip in the bud" means:
o: To stop something at an early stage
e: The problem is stopped before it grows.

q: The interviewer tried to ______ a response from the witness.
e: "Elicit" means to draw out; "illicit" means illegal.

q: The new rule will ______ everyone in the office.
e: "Affect" is the verb; "effect" is usually the noun.

q: The medicine had no ______ on him.
e: "Effect" is the noun meaning "result".

q: A judge must be ______ , with no personal stake in the case.
e: "Disinterested" means impartial; "uninterested" means not interested.

q: She was ______ in the lecture and fell asleep.
e: "Uninterested" means bored or not interested.

q: The doctor will ______ a course of antibiotics.
e: "Prescribe" means to order as treatment; "proscribe" means to forbid.

q: The law ______ the sale of such drugs.
e: "Proscribe" means to forbid.

q: He likes to ______ his wealth.
e: "Flaunt" means to show off; "flout" means to defy openly.

q: They openly ______ the traffic rules.
e: "Flout" means to treat rules with contempt.

q: The mountain road was long and ______ .
e: "Tortuous" means full of twists; "torturous" means causing torture.

q: It was an ______ device, cleverly made.
e: "Ingenious" means clever; "ingenuous" means innocent and frank.

q: The ______ of the college addressed the students.
e: A "principal" is a head; a "principle" is a rule.

q: He is a man of high ______ .
e: "Principles" are moral rules.

q: I cannot ______ your offer.
e: "Accept" means to receive; "except" means leaving out.

q: Everyone came ______ Ali.
e: "Except" means "but not".

q: Please ______ me on this legal matter.
e: "Advise" is the verb; "advice" is the noun.

q: The weather may ______ our plans.
e: "Alter" means to change; an "altar" is a table in a place of worship.

q: The desert has a hot, dry ______ .
e: "Climate" is the general weather of a region.

q: The ship was a ______ vessel that did not move.
e: "Stationary" means not moving; "stationery" is writing material.

q: He bought paper and pens from the ______ shop.
e: "Stationery" means writing materials.

q: The dog wagged ______ tail.
e: "Its" is the possessive; "it's" means "it is".

q: The two brothers ______ each other in looks.
e: "Resemble" takes a direct object with no preposition.

q: We must ______ our differences and work together.
e: "Reconcile" means to settle.

q: The account sounded plausible; only a ______ reader would accept it without proof.
e: "Credulous" means too ready to believe; "credible" means believable.

q: His story was so ______ that everyone believed it.
e: "Credible" means believable.

q: The old ruins ______ a vanished era.
e: "Evoke" means to bring to mind; "invoke" means to call upon.

q: The minister had to ______ the order after the protest.
e: "Revoke" means to cancel officially.

q: The ______ of the story is that honesty pays.
e: A "moral" is a lesson; "morale" is the spirit of a group.

q: The team's ______ was high after the victory.
e: "Morale" means confidence and spirit.

q: The flood caused ______ damage to the crops.
e: "Extensive" means large in amount or area.

q: According to Passage 1, the main reason a city stays hot at night is that:
o: Fields absorb the city's cool air
Building materials release stored heat slowly
The sun shines longer over cities
Trees give off heat after dark
e: The passage says concrete and asphalt give heat back slowly after dark.

q: In Passage 1, the word "remedies" most nearly means:
e: A remedy is a means of putting something right.

q: Which statement would the author of Passage 1 most likely accept?
o: Tall buildings help cool the streets
Only expensive technology can cool cities
Simple measures can save lives during heatwaves
e: The last sentence says the difference can decide survival.

q: Pale roofs help, according to Passage 1, because they:
e: Pale surfaces "throw sunlight back instead of storing it".

q: The best title for Passage 1 would be:
o: Why Cities Overheat and What Helps
e: The passage explains the cause of urban heat and two remedies.

q: The central claim of Passage 2 is that:
o: Enumerators do not follow their manuals
Census figures depend on definitions that must be checked before comparing them
e: The passage argues that totals rest on prior definitions.

q: In Passage 2, the choices behind a census are described as "not hidden" because they:
o: Are the same in every country
e: The passage says they are printed in the enumerator's manual.

q: According to Passage 2, an apparent rise in urbanisation may be misleading when:
o: The definition of "urban" has changed between counts
e: A widened definition creates change on paper only.

q: The "careful reader" in Passage 2 is advised to:
o: Ask whether the same thing was counted both times
e: The last sentence gives this advice.

q: The tone of Passage 2 is best described as:
e: The author warns the reader to be careful.

q: According to Passage 3, old letters were written carefully mainly because:
o: Mistakes could not be corrected quickly
e: There was "no chance to correct a misunderstanding".

q: The merchant sent a second copy of his letter in order to:
o: Guard against loss of the first
e: The copy went by another ship "in case the first was lost".

q: In Passage 3, "reversed" most nearly means:
e: Speed has produced the opposite habits.

q: The author's attitude to fast communication in Passage 3 is:
o: Balanced: it brings gains and a loss
e: The author says "we have gained much" but notes one lost advantage.

q: The main idea of Passage 3 is that:
o: The speed of communication shapes how carefully people write
Merchants were more honest in the past
e: The passage contrasts habits under slow and fast communication.

q: According to Passage 4, a good water agreement should:
o: Fix shares by rule and create a joint body that meets regularly
Give all water to the upstream country
e: The passage names these two elements.

q: The author of Passage 4 regards the joint body of engineers as:
o: More important than the sharing formula
e: It is called "the less noticed but the more important".

q: In Passage 4, "entitlement" most nearly means:
e: Each side knows what it has a right to receive.

q: A fixed formula alone is not enough, according to Passage 4, because:
e: It "cannot foresee the floods, droughts and new works of the next".

q: The opening sentence of Passage 4 means that:
e: Water flows across the borders that people draw.

q: The author of Passage 5 believes that memory and understanding are:
o: Both necessary and dependent on each other
e: They are called "partners".

q: The author of Passage 5 rejects which pair of views?
o: That terms must be known, and that arguments use terms
That examinations test only memory, and that memory has no value
That facts are bricks, and that plans are needed
That students learn dates, and that events have causes
e: The first charge is only "partly fair" and the opposite complaint is "equally mistaken".

q: In the comparison used in Passage 5, "the plan" stands for:
e: "Understanding is the plan by which they are put together."

q: In Passage 5, the phrase "the charge is partly fair" means the criticism is:
e: "Partly fair" means true in part.

q: According to Passage 5, a student who cannot recall when events happened cannot:
e: The passage says such a student "cannot judge which caused which".

q: Simplify: 29 + 9 × 4 − 9 ÷ 3
e: Multiply and divide first: 9 × 4 = 36 and 9 ÷ 3 = 3. Then 29 + 36 − 3 = 62.

q: Simplify: 22 + 8 × 8 − 6 ÷ 3
e: Multiply and divide first: 8 × 8 = 64 and 6 ÷ 3 = 2. Then 22 + 64 − 2 = 84.

q: Simplify: 25 + 3 × 3 − 30 ÷ 5
e: Multiply and divide first: 3 × 3 = 9 and 30 ÷ 5 = 6. Then 25 + 9 − 6 = 28.

q: What is the least common multiple (LCM) of 25, 6 and 24?
e: Take the highest power of each prime factor of 25, 6 and 24. The LCM is 600.

q: What is the least common multiple (LCM) of 30, 4 and 10?
e: Take the highest power of each prime factor of 30, 4 and 10. The LCM is 60.

q: The HCF of two numbers is 9 and their LCM is 189. If one number is 27, what is the other?
e: Product of two numbers = HCF × LCM. Other number = 9 × 189 ÷ 27 = 63.

q: The HCF of two numbers is 14 and their LCM is 420. If one number is 70, what is the other?
e: Product of two numbers = HCF × LCM. Other number = 14 × 420 ÷ 70 = 84.

q: If 4^k = 8, what is the value of k?
e: Write both sides as powers of 2: 2^(2k) = 2^3. So 2k = 3 and k = 3/2.

q: If 16^k = 8, what is the value of k?
e: Write both sides as powers of 2: 2^(4k) = 2^3. So 4k = 3 and k = 3/4.

q: If 32^k = 8, what is the value of k?
e: Write both sides as powers of 2: 2^(5k) = 2^3. So 5k = 3 and k = 3/5.

q: How many prime numbers are there less than 50?
How many prime numbers are there less than 40?
A man spends 1/2 of his salary on rent and 1/4 on food. He is left with Rs 5,000. What is his salary?
e: Fraction left = 1 − 1/2 − 1/4 = 1/4. So 1/4 of the salary = 5,000, and the salary = 5,000 ÷ 1/4 = Rs 20,000.

q: A man spends 1/3 of his salary on rent and 1/5 on food. He is left with Rs 21,000. What is his salary?
e: Fraction left = 1 − 1/3 − 1/5 = 7/15. So 7/15 of the salary = 21,000, and the salary = 21,000 ÷ 7/15 = Rs 45,000.

q: A man spends 1/3 of his salary on rent and 1/4 on food. He is left with Rs 25,000. What is his salary?
e: Fraction left = 1 − 1/3 − 1/4 = 5/12. So 5/12 of the salary = 25,000, and the salary = 25,000 ÷ 5/12 = Rs 60,000.

q: What is the value of 71² − 63²?
What is the value of 81² − 71²?
What is the smallest number that must be added to 2,016 to make it exactly divisible by 11?
e: 2,016 ÷ 11 leaves remainder 3. Add 11 − 3 = 8.

q: What is the smallest number that must be added to 495 to make it exactly divisible by 13?
e: 495 ÷ 13 leaves remainder 1. Add 13 − 1 = 12.

q: If 75% of a number is 1,350, what is the number?
If 8% of a number is 144, what is the number?
If 35% of a number is 385, what is the number?
A price is increased by 30% and the new price is then reduced by 10%. What is the net change?
e: Multiply the factors: 1.3 × 0.9 = 1.17. Net change: 17% increase.

q: A price is increased by 50% and the new price is then reduced by 20%. What is the net change?
e: Multiply the factors: 1.5 × 0.8 = 1.2. Net change: 20% increase.

q: A price is increased by 20% and the new price is then reduced by 10%. What is the net change?
e: Multiply the factors: 1.2 × 0.9 = 1.08. Net change: 8% increase.

q: A shop sold 15% of its stock of bulbs and had 3,995 bulbs left. How many bulbs did it have at first?
e: The 3,995 bulbs are 85% of the stock. Stock = 3,995 × 100 ÷ 85 = 4,700.

q: A shop sold 45% of its stock of bulbs and had 1,925 bulbs left. How many bulbs did it have at first?
e: The 1,925 bulbs are 55% of the stock. Stock = 1,925 × 100 ÷ 55 = 3,500.

q: A shop sold 35% of its stock of bulbs and had 1,365 bulbs left. How many bulbs did it have at first?
e: The 1,365 bulbs are 65% of the stock. Stock = 1,365 × 100 ÷ 65 = 2,100.

q: A's salary is 25% more than B's. By what percentage is B's salary less than A's?
e: Let B = 100, so A = 125. B is less by 25 out of 125, which is 20%.

q: A's salary is 60% more than B's. By what percentage is B's salary less than A's?
e: Let B = 100, so A = 160. B is less by 60 out of 160, which is 37.5%.

q: In an election between two candidates, the winner got 70% of the valid votes and won by 13,600 votes. How many valid votes were cast?
e: The loser got 30%. The margin is 70% − 30% = 40% of the votes = 13,600. Total = 13,600 × 100 ÷ 40 = 34,000.

q: In an election between two candidates, the winner got 60% of the valid votes and won by 2,700 votes. How many valid votes were cast?
e: The loser got 40%. The margin is 60% − 40% = 20% of the votes = 2,700. Total = 2,700 × 100 ÷ 20 = 13,500.

q: In an election between two candidates, the winner got 58% of the valid votes and won by 5,120 votes. How many valid votes were cast?
e: The loser got 42%. The margin is 58% − 42% = 16% of the votes = 5,120. Total = 5,120 × 100 ÷ 16 = 32,000.

q: The population of a town is 300,000. It grows by 20% every year. What will it be after two years?
e: After year 1: 360,000. After year 2: add 20% again to get 432,000. Simple addition of 40% gives the wrong answer 420,000.

q: The population of a town is 120,000. It grows by 10% every year. What will it be after two years?
e: After year 1: 132,000. After year 2: add 10% again to get 145,200. Simple addition of 20% gives the wrong answer 144,000.

q: A student needs 33% marks to pass. He gets 119 marks and fails by 13 marks. What are the maximum marks?
e: Pass marks = 119 + 13 = 132. This is 33% of the maximum, so maximum = 132 × 100 ÷ 33 = 400.

q: A student needs 33% marks to pass. He gets 243 marks and fails by 21 marks. What are the maximum marks?
e: Pass marks = 243 + 21 = 264. This is 33% of the maximum, so maximum = 264 × 100 ÷ 33 = 800.

q: A student needs 35% marks to pass. He gets 235 marks and fails by 10 marks. What are the maximum marks?
e: Pass marks = 235 + 10 = 245. This is 35% of the maximum, so maximum = 245 × 100 ÷ 35 = 700.

q: An article bought for Rs 2,450 is sold for Rs 3,185. What is the profit or loss per cent?
e: Profit = 735. Per cent on cost = 735 ÷ 2,450 × 100 = 30%. Always divide by the cost price.

q: An article bought for Rs 1,000 is sold for Rs 1,400. What is the profit or loss per cent?
e: Profit = 400. Per cent on cost = 400 ÷ 1,000 × 100 = 40%. Always divide by the cost price.

q: An article bought for Rs 1,450 is sold for Rs 1,305. What is the profit or loss per cent?
e: Loss = 145. Per cent on cost = 145 ÷ 1,450 × 100 = 10%. Always divide by the cost price.

q: After a discount of 25%, an article is sold for Rs 3,300. What is its marked price?
e: Selling price is 75% of the marked price. Marked price = 3,300 × 100 ÷ 75 = Rs 4,400.

q: After a discount of 40%, an article is sold for Rs 1,860. What is its marked price?
e: Selling price is 60% of the marked price. Marked price = 1,860 × 100 ÷ 60 = Rs 3,100.

q: After a discount of 40%, an article is sold for Rs 420. What is its marked price?
e: Selling price is 60% of the marked price. Marked price = 420 × 100 ÷ 60 = Rs 700.

q: The cost price of 16 articles is equal to the selling price of 20 articles. What is the profit or loss per cent?
e: Let the cost of one article be Re 1. Then 20 articles cost 20 and sell for 16. Loss = 4 on 20 = 20%.

q: The cost price of 20 articles is equal to the selling price of 25 articles. What is the profit or loss per cent?
e: Let the cost of one article be Re 1. Then 25 articles cost 25 and sell for 20. Loss = 5 on 25 = 20%.

q: The cost price of 15 articles is equal to the selling price of 10 articles. What is the profit or loss per cent?
e: Let the cost of one article be Re 1. Then 10 articles cost 10 and sell for 15. Profit = 5 on 10 = 50%.

q: Two successive discounts of 20% and 50% are equal to a single discount of:
e: Single discount = a + b − ab/100 = 20 + 50 − 10 = 60%.

q: Two successive discounts of 15% and 30% are equal to a single discount of:
e: Single discount = a + b − ab/100 = 15 + 30 − 4.5 = 40.5%.

q: Two successive discounts of 10% and 10% are equal to a single discount of:
e: Single discount = a + b − ab/100 = 10 + 10 − 1 = 19%.

q: A trader sells an article at a loss of 10%. Had he sold it for Rs 150 more, he would have gained 15%. What is the cost price?
e: The extra Rs 150 covers the gap from −10% to +15%, which is 25% of the cost. Cost = 150 × 100 ÷ 25 = Rs 600.

q: A trader sells an article at a loss of 15%. Had he sold it for Rs 100 more, he would have gained 10%. What is the cost price?
e: The extra Rs 100 covers the gap from −15% to +10%, which is 25% of the cost. Cost = 100 × 100 ÷ 25 = Rs 400.

q: What is the simple interest on Rs 13,500 at 8% per year for 3 years?
Rs 16,500 earns Rs 2,475 as simple interest in 3 years. What is the rate per year?
Rs 11,500 earns Rs 2,760 as simple interest in 4 years. What is the rate per year?
Rs 1,500 earns Rs 360 as simple interest in 4 years. What is the rate per year?
What is the compound interest on Rs 8,000 at 10% per year for 2 years, compounded yearly?
What is the difference between compound and simple interest on Rs 20,000 for 2 years at 5% per year?
e: For 2 years the difference is P × (R/100)² = 20,000 × (5/100)² = Rs 50.

q: What is the difference between compound and simple interest on Rs 12,000 for 2 years at 20% per year?
e: For 2 years the difference is P × (R/100)² = 12,000 × (20/100)² = Rs 480.

q: Rs 25,200 is divided among three people in the ratio 2 : 7 : 9. What is the largest share?
e: Total parts = 18. One part = 25,200 ÷ 18 = 1,400. The largest share = 9 × 1,400 = Rs 12,600.

q: Rs 34,800 is divided among three people in the ratio 2 : 3 : 7. What is the smallest share?
e: Total parts = 12. One part = 34,800 ÷ 12 = 2,900. The smallest share = 2 × 2,900 = Rs 5,800.

q: Rs 30,000 is divided among three people in the ratio 4 : 5 : 6. What is the smallest share?
e: Total parts = 15. One part = 30,000 ÷ 15 = 2,000. The smallest share = 4 × 2,000 = Rs 8,000.

q: The ratio of boys to girls in a school is 4 : 3. There are 8 more boys than girls. How many students are there in all?
e: Difference of parts = 1 = 8 students, so one part = 8. Total = 7 parts = 56.

q: The ratio of boys to girls in a school is 8 : 5. There are 12 more boys than girls. How many students are there in all?
e: Difference of parts = 3 = 12 students, so one part = 4. Total = 13 parts = 52.

q: The ratio of boys to girls in a school is 8 : 5. There are 63 more boys than girls. How many students are there in all?
e: Difference of parts = 3 = 63 students, so one part = 21. Total = 13 parts = 273.

q: A 16-litre mixture contains milk and water in the ratio 3 : 1. How much water must be added to make the ratio 3 : 3?
e: Milk = 12 litres, water = 4 litres. Milk stays the same, so water must become 12 litres. Add 12 − 4 = 8 litres.

q: A 40-litre mixture contains milk and water in the ratio 3 : 1. How much water must be added to make the ratio 3 : 2?
e: Milk = 30 litres, water = 10 litres. Milk stays the same, so water must become 20 litres. Add 20 − 10 = 10 litres.

q: A 75-litre mixture contains milk and water in the ratio 3 : 2. How much water must be added to make the ratio 3 : 3?
e: Milk = 45 litres, water = 30 litres. Milk stays the same, so water must become 45 litres. Add 45 − 30 = 15 litres.

q: If 16 notebooks cost Rs 240, what do 30 notebooks cost at the same rate?
e: One notebook costs 240 ÷ 16 = Rs 15. So 30 cost 30 × 15 = Rs 450.

q: If 6 notebooks cost Rs 360, what do 40 notebooks cost at the same rate?
e: One notebook costs 360 ÷ 6 = Rs 60. So 40 cost 40 × 60 = Rs 2,400.

q: On a map, 1 cm represents 25 km. Two towns are 7.5 cm apart on the map. What is the real distance between them?
e: Distance = 7.5 × 25 = 187.5 km.

q: On a map, 1 cm represents 40 km. Two towns are 2.4 cm apart on the map. What is the real distance between them?
e: Distance = 2.4 × 40 = 96 km.

q: If A : B = 2 : 3 and B : C = 4 : 5, what is A : B : C?
e: Make B the same in both ratios (LCM of 3 and 4 is 12). The combined ratio is 8 : 12 : 15.

q: If A : B = 2 : 5 and B : C = 3 : 7, what is A : B : C?
e: Make B the same in both ratios (LCM of 5 and 3 is 15). The combined ratio is 6 : 15 : 35.

q: The average of 10 numbers is 55. When one more number is included, the average becomes 53. What is the new number?
e: Old total = 10 × 55 = 550. New total = 11 × 53 = 583. New number = 583 − 550 = 33.

q: The average of 6 numbers is 31. When one more number is included, the average becomes 29. What is the new number?
e: Old total = 6 × 31 = 186. New total = 7 × 29 = 203. New number = 203 − 186 = 17.

q: The average of 8 numbers is 30. When one more number is included, the average becomes 29. What is the new number?
e: Old total = 8 × 30 = 240. New total = 9 × 29 = 261. New number = 261 − 240 = 21.

q: In a class, 40 boys have an average score of 62 and 10 girls have an average score of 77. What is the average score of the whole class?
e: Total = 40 × 62 + 10 × 77 = 3250. Divide by 50 students: 65. The simple mean of 62 and 77 is wrong because the groups are unequal.

q: In a class, 20 boys have an average score of 41 and 30 girls have an average score of 71. What is the average score of the whole class?
e: Total = 20 × 41 + 30 × 71 = 2950. Divide by 50 students: 59. The simple mean of 41 and 71 is wrong because the groups are unequal.

q: In a class, 18 boys have an average score of 73 and 12 girls have an average score of 48. What is the average score of the whole class?
e: Total = 18 × 73 + 12 × 48 = 1890. Divide by 30 students: 63. The simple mean of 73 and 48 is wrong because the groups are unequal.

q: A car travels from A to B at 40 km/h and returns over the same road at 120 km/h. What is its average speed for the whole journey?
e: For equal distances, average speed = 2uv ÷ (u + v) = 2 × 40 × 120 ÷ 160 = 60 km/h. It is not the simple mean 80.

q: A car travels from A to B at 24 km/h and returns over the same road at 40 km/h. What is its average speed for the whole journey?
e: For equal distances, average speed = 2uv ÷ (u + v) = 2 × 24 × 40 ÷ 64 = 30 km/h. It is not the simple mean 32.

q: A car travels from A to B at 30 km/h and returns over the same road at 45 km/h. What is its average speed for the whole journey?
e: For equal distances, average speed = 2uv ÷ (u + v) = 2 × 30 × 45 ÷ 75 = 36 km/h. It is not the simple mean 37.5.

q: A batsman has an average of 26 runs over 12 innings. He scores 39 in the next innings. What is his new average?
e: New total = 12 × 26 + 39 = 351. New average = 351 ÷ 13 = 27.

q: A batsman has an average of 32 runs over 17 innings. He scores 68 in the next innings. What is his new average?
e: New total = 17 × 32 + 68 = 612. New average = 612 ÷ 18 = 34.

q: The arithmetic mean of 8, 4, 27, 25 and x is 20. What is the value of x?
e: Total must be 5 × 20 = 100. The four known numbers add up to 64. So x = 100 − 64 = 36.

q: The arithmetic mean of 24, 16, 7, 16 and x is 16. What is the value of x?
e: Total must be 5 × 16 = 80. The four known numbers add up to 63. So x = 80 − 63 = 17.

q: The average weight of 8 people rises by 2 kg when one of them, who weighs 53 kg, is replaced by a new person. What is the weight of the new person?
e: The total rises by 8 × 2 = 16 kg. New person = 53 + 16 = 69 kg.

q: The average weight of 5 people rises by 2 kg when one of them, who weighs 43 kg, is replaced by a new person. What is the weight of the new person?
e: The total rises by 5 × 2 = 10 kg. New person = 43 + 10 = 53 kg.

q: Asad is 4 times as old as Bina. In 4 years, the sum of their ages will be 33. How old is Asad now?
e: Let Bina be x. Then 4x + x + 2 × 4 = 33, so 5x = 25 and x = 5. Asad is 4 × 5 = 20.

q: Asad is 3 times as old as Bina. In 9 years, the sum of their ages will be 58. How old is Asad now?
e: Let Bina be x. Then 3x + x + 2 × 9 = 58, so 4x = 40 and x = 10. Asad is 3 × 10 = 30.

q: Asad is 4 times as old as Bina. In 5 years, the sum of their ages will be 70. How old is Asad now?
e: Let Bina be x. Then 4x + x + 2 × 5 = 70, so 5x = 60 and x = 12. Asad is 4 × 12 = 48.

q: The ages of two brothers are in the ratio 7 : 5 and add up to 72 years. How old will the elder brother be after 6 years?
e: One part = 72 ÷ 12 = 6. The elder is 7 × 6 = 42 now and will be 48 after 6 years.

q: The ages of two brothers are in the ratio 7 : 5 and add up to 60 years. How old will the elder brother be after 7 years?
e: One part = 60 ÷ 12 = 5. The elder is 7 × 5 = 35 now and will be 42 after 7 years.

q: The ages of two brothers are in the ratio 5 : 3 and add up to 56 years. How old will the elder brother be after 5 years?
e: One part = 56 ÷ 8 = 7. The elder is 5 × 7 = 35 now and will be 40 after 5 years.

q: A father is now 3 times as old as his son. After 8 years he will be 2 times as old as his son. How old is the father now?
e: Let the son be x. Then 3x + 8 = 2(x + 8), so x = 8 and x = 8. The father is 3 × 8 = 24.

q: A father is now 5 times as old as his son. After 8 years he will be 3 times as old as his son. How old is the father now?
e: Let the son be x. Then 5x + 8 = 3(x + 8), so 2x = 16 and x = 8. The father is 5 × 8 = 40.

q: A father is now 7 times as old as his son. After 8 years he will be 3 times as old as his son. How old is the father now?
e: Let the son be x. Then 7x + 8 = 3(x + 8), so 4x = 16 and x = 4. The father is 7 × 4 = 28.

q: For what value of x is 6(x − 1) + 1 = 1x + 35?
e: Expand: 6x − 6 + 1 = 1x + 35. So 5x = 40 and x = 8.

q: For what value of x is 3(x − 7) + 1 = 2x − 18?
e: Expand: 3x − 21 + 1 = 2x − 18. So 1x = 2 and x = 2.

q: For what value of x is 4(x − 8) + 1 = 1x − 7?
e: Expand: 4x − 32 + 1 = 1x − 7. So 3x = 24 and x = 8.

q: 3 pens and 5 pencils cost Rs 169. 3 pens and 2 pencils cost Rs 127. What is the cost of one pen?
e: Solve 3x + 5y = 169 and 3x + 2y = 127. Eliminating y gives x = 33 (and y = 14). One pen costs Rs 33.

q: 1 pens and 5 pencils cost Rs 126. 2 pens and 1 pencils cost Rs 81. What is the cost of one pen?
e: Solve 1x + 5y = 126 and 2x + 1y = 81. Eliminating y gives x = 31 (and y = 19). One pen costs Rs 31.

q: 5 pens and 1 pencils cost Rs 164. 2 pens and 5 pencils cost Rs 130. What is the cost of one pen?
e: Solve 5x + 1y = 164 and 2x + 5y = 130. Eliminating y gives x = 30 (and y = 14). One pen costs Rs 30.

q: What are the roots of x² − 3x − 18 = 0?
e: The roots must add up to 3 and multiply to −18. The numbers −3 and 6 do both.

q: What are the roots of x² − 3x − 10 = 0?
e: The roots must add up to 3 and multiply to −10. The numbers −2 and 5 do both.

q: What are the roots of x² − 8x + 12 = 0?
e: The roots must add up to 8 and multiply to 12. The numbers 2 and 6 do both.

q: If a + b = 15 and ab = 50, what is the value of a² + b²?
If a + b = 12 and ab = 11, what is the value of a² + b²?
If x + 1/x = 3, what is the value of x² + 1/x²?
e: Square both sides: x² + 2 + 1/x² = 9. So x² + 1/x² = 9 − 2 = 7.

q: If x − 1/x = 4, what is the value of x² + 1/x²?
e: Square both sides: x² − 2 + 1/x² = 16. So x² + 1/x² = 16 + 2 = 18.

q: The sum of three consecutive even numbers is 36. What is the largest of them?
e: The middle number is 36 ÷ 3 = 12. The three numbers are 10, 12, 14, so the largest is 14.

q: The sum of three consecutive odd numbers is 171. What is the largest of them?
e: The middle number is 171 ÷ 3 = 57. The three numbers are 55, 57, 59, so the largest is 59.

q: The sum of four consecutive whole numbers is 78. What is the smallest of them?
e: Let them be n, n+1, n+2, n+3. Then 4n + 6 = 78, so n = 18.

q: A number is multiplied by 3 and then 20 is subtracted. The result is 52. What is the number?
A number is multiplied by 5 and then 10 is subtracted. The result is 60. What is the number?
How many integers n satisfy −15 < 2n ≤ 18?
e: Divide by 2: −7.5 < n ≤ 9. The integers are −7 to 9, which is 17 values.

q: How many integers n satisfy −12 < 2n ≤ 13?
e: Divide by 2: −6 < n ≤ 6.5. The integers are −5 to 6, which is 12 values.

q: x² + 10x + 0 is written in the form (x + a)² + b. What is the value of b?
e: Half of 10 is 5, so (x + 5)² = x² + 10x + 25. Then b = 0 − 25 = −25.

q: x² + 16x + 9 is written in the form (x + a)² + b. What is the value of b?
e: Half of 16 is 8, so (x + 8)² = x² + 16x + 64. Then b = 9 − 64 = −55.

q: The angles of a triangle are in the ratio 1 : 3 : 5. What is the largest angle?
e: The angles add up to 180°. One part = 180 ÷ 9 = 20°. Largest = 5 × 20 = 100°.

q: The angles of a triangle are in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3. What is the largest angle?
e: The angles add up to 180°. One part = 180 ÷ 6 = 30°. Largest = 3 × 30 = 90°.

q: Two angles of a triangle measure 47° and 82°. What is the third angle?
Two angles of a triangle measure 50° and 49°. What is the third angle?
What is the size of each interior angle of a regular polygon with 8 sides?
e: Sum of interior angles = (8 − 2) × 180° = 1080°. Each angle = 1080 ÷ 8 = 135°.

q: What is the size of each interior angle of a regular polygon with 9 sides?
e: Sum of interior angles = (9 − 2) × 180° = 1260°. Each angle = 1260 ÷ 9 = 140°.

q: Each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 45°. How many sides does it have?
e: Exterior angles add up to 360°. Sides = 360 ÷ 45 = 8.

q: The length of a rectangle is four times its width and its perimeter is 140 m. What is its area?
e: Let the width be w. Then 2(4w + w) = 140, so w = 14 m and the length is 56 m. Area = 56 × 14 = 784 m².

q: The length of a rectangle is twice its width and its perimeter is 18 m. What is its area?
e: Let the width be w. Then 2(2w + w) = 18, so w = 3 m and the length is 6 m. Area = 6 × 3 = 18 m².

q: The circumference of a circle is 88 cm. What is its area? (Take π = 22/7.)
e: 2πr = 88, so r = 14 cm. Area = πr² = 22/7 × 14² = 616 cm².

q: The area of a circle is 1,386 cm². What is its radius? (Take π = 22/7.)
The circumference of a circle is 132 cm. What is its area? (Take π = 22/7.)
e: 2πr = 132, so r = 21 cm. Area = πr² = 22/7 × 21² = 1,386 cm².

q: A rectangular water tank is 1.2 m long, 0.8 m wide and 50 cm deep. How many litres of water can it hold?
e: Volume = 1.2 × 0.8 × 0.5 = 0.48 m³. One cubic metre is 1,000 litres, so the tank holds 480 litres.

q: A rectangular water tank is 2 m long, 2 m wide and 120 cm deep. How many litres of water can it hold?
e: Volume = 2 × 2 × 1.2 = 4.8 m³. One cubic metre is 1,000 litres, so the tank holds 4,800 litres.

q: What is the curved surface area of a cylinder of radius 14 cm and height 8 cm? (Take π = 22/7.)
e: Curved surface area = 2πrh = 2 × 22/7 × 14 × 8 = 704 cm².

q: What is the volume of a cylinder of radius 14 cm and height 8 cm? (Take π = 22/7.)
e: Volume = πr²h = 22/7 × 14² × 8 = 4,928 cm³.

q: What is the volume of a cylinder of radius 10.5 cm and height 20 cm? (Take π = 22/7.)
e: Volume = πr²h = 22/7 × 10.5² × 20 = 6,930 cm³.

q: A ladder 5 m long leans against a wall with its foot 3 m from the wall. How high up the wall does it reach?
e: Height² = 5² − 3² = 16, so the height is 4 m.

q: The foot of a ladder is 5 m from a wall and its top reaches 12 m up the wall. How long is the ladder?
e: Length² = 5² + 12² = 169, so the ladder is 13 m long.

q: A ladder 29 m long leans against a wall with its foot 20 m from the wall. How high up the wall does it reach?
e: Height² = 29² − 20² = 441, so the height is 21 m.

q: A wheel has a diameter of 35 cm. How many complete turns does it make in covering 220 m? (Take π = 22/7.)
e: Circumference = πd = 22/7 × 35 = 110 cm = 1.1 m. Turns = 220 ÷ 1.1 = 200.

q: A wheel has a diameter of 28 cm. How many complete turns does it make in covering 880 m? (Take π = 22/7.)
e: Circumference = πd = 22/7 × 28 = 88 cm = 0.88 m. Turns = 880 ÷ 0.88 = 1000.

q: The diagonal of a square is 20 cm. What is its area?
e: Area of a square = diagonal² ÷ 2 = 400 ÷ 2 = 200 cm².

q: The perimeter of a square is 116 cm. What is its area?
e: Side = 116 ÷ 4 = 29 cm. Area = 29² = 841 cm².

q: Each side of a square is increased by 30%. By what percentage does its area change?
e: Area factor = (1.3)² = 1.69. The area increases by 69%.

q: Each side of a square is decreased by 10%. By what percentage does its area change?
e: Area factor = (0.9)² = 0.81. The area decreases by 19%.

q: A can finish a job in 9 days and B can finish it in 18 days. How long will they take working together?
e: In one day they do 1/9 + 1/18 = 1/6 of the job. Time = 6 days. Shortcut: ab ÷ (a + b).

q: A can finish a job in 18 days and B can finish it in 36 days. How long will they take working together?
e: In one day they do 1/18 + 1/36 = 1/12 of the job. Time = 12 days. Shortcut: ab ÷ (a + b).

q: A can finish a job in 6 days and B can finish it in 3 days. How long will they take working together?
e: In one day they do 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2 of the job. Time = 2 days. Shortcut: ab ÷ (a + b).

q: 15 men can finish a piece of work in 24 days. How long will 36 men take to finish the same work?
e: Work = 15 × 24 = 360 man-days. Time for 36 men = 360 ÷ 36 = 10 days. More men, fewer days.

q: 12 men can finish a piece of work in 15 days. How long will 36 men take to finish the same work?
e: Work = 12 × 15 = 180 man-days. Time for 36 men = 180 ÷ 36 = 5 days. More men, fewer days.

q: 18 men can finish a piece of work in 10 days. How long will 20 men take to finish the same work?
e: Work = 18 × 10 = 180 man-days. Time for 20 men = 180 ÷ 20 = 9 days. More men, fewer days.

q: A group of workers can finish a job in 24 days. If 15 workers are absent, the rest finish it in 96 days. How many workers are in the full group?
e: Let the group be x. Then 24x = 96(x − 15), so 72x = 1440 and x = 20.

q: A group of workers can finish a job in 10 days. If 6 workers are absent, the rest finish it in 12 days. How many workers are in the full group?
e: Let the group be x. Then 10x = 12(x − 6), so 2x = 72 and x = 36.

q: One pipe fills a tank in 6 hours and another fills it in 3 hours. How long do they take together?
e: In one hour they fill 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2 of the tank. Time = 2 hours.

q: One pipe fills a tank in 12 hours and another fills it in 24 hours. How long do they take together?
e: In one hour they fill 1/12 + 1/24 = 1/8 of the tank. Time = 8 hours.

q: A tap can fill a tank in 6 hours and a drain can empty the full tank in 12 hours. If both are open, how long will it take to fill the empty tank?
e: Net filling in one hour = 1/6 − 1/12 = 1/12. Time = 12 hours.

q: A and B together finish a job in 18 days. A alone can finish it in 30 days. How long would B take alone?
e: B's daily work = 1/18 − 1/30 = 1/45. So B needs 45 days.

q: A and B together finish a job in 10 days. A alone can finish it in 15 days. How long would B take alone?
e: B's daily work = 1/10 − 1/15 = 1/30. So B needs 30 days.

q: A train 100 m long runs at 36 km/h. How long does it take to pass a platform 100 m long?
e: Speed = 36 × 5/18 = 10 m/s. Distance = 100 + 100 = 200 m. Time = 200 ÷ 10 = 20 seconds.

q: A train 180 m long runs at 108 km/h. How long does it take to pass a platform 300 m long?
e: Speed = 108 × 5/18 = 30 m/s. Distance = 180 + 300 = 480 m. Time = 480 ÷ 30 = 16 seconds.

q: A train 140 m long passes a signal post in 8 seconds. What is its speed in km/h?
e: Speed = 140 ÷ 8 = 35/2 m/s. Multiply by 18/5 to get 63 km/h.

q: Two trains start at the same time from stations 360 km apart and travel towards each other at 55 km/h and 65 km/h. After how long do they meet?
e: They close the gap at 55 + 65 = 120 km/h. Time = 360 ÷ 120 = 3 hours.

q: Two trains start at the same time from stations 160 km apart and travel towards each other at 30 km/h and 50 km/h. After how long do they meet?
e: They close the gap at 30 + 50 = 80 km/h. Time = 160 ÷ 80 = 2 hours.

q: A car covers 110 km in 2 hours 45 minutes at a steady speed. What is its speed?
e: Time = 11/4 hours. Speed = 110 ÷ 11/4 = 40 km/h.

q: A car covers 60 km in 1 hours 30 minutes at a steady speed. What is its speed?
e: Time = 3/2 hours. Speed = 60 ÷ 3/2 = 40 km/h.

q: A boat travels at 18 km/h downstream and 10 km/h upstream. What is the speed of the current?
e: Current = (downstream − upstream) ÷ 2 = (18 − 10) ÷ 2 = 4 km/h.

q: A boat travels at 18 km/h downstream and 6 km/h upstream. What is its speed in still water?
e: Still-water speed = (downstream + upstream) ÷ 2 = (18 + 6) ÷ 2 = 12 km/h.

q: A thief is 1,200 m ahead of a policeman. The thief runs at 11 km/h and the policeman at 15 km/h. How long does the policeman take to catch him?
e: The gap closes at 15 − 11 = 4 km/h. Time = 1.2 km ÷ 4 km/h = 3/10 hour = 18 minutes.

q: A thief is 200 m ahead of a policeman. The thief runs at 11 km/h and the policeman at 13 km/h. How long does the policeman take to catch him?
e: The gap closes at 13 − 11 = 2 km/h. Time = 0.2 km ÷ 2 km/h = 1/10 hour = 6 minutes.

q: In a 200 m race, Ali finishes in 40 seconds and Babar in 50 seconds, each at a steady speed. By what distance does Ali beat Babar?
e: In 40 seconds Babar covers 200 × 40 ÷ 50 = 160 m. Ali wins by 200 − 160 = 40 m.

q: In a 200 m race, Ali finishes in 27 seconds and Babar in 30 seconds, each at a steady speed. By what distance does Ali beat Babar?
e: In 27 seconds Babar covers 200 × 27 ÷ 30 = 180 m. Ali wins by 200 − 180 = 20 m.

q: In a group of 80 people, 44 like tea, 25 like coffee and 5 like both. How many like neither?
e: At least one = 44 + 25 − 5 = 64. Neither = 80 − 64 = 16.

q: In a group of 100 people, 52 like tea, 47 like coffee and 21 like both. How many like neither?
e: At least one = 52 + 47 − 21 = 78. Neither = 100 − 78 = 22.

q: In a group of 200 people, 89 like tea, 96 like coffee and 73 like both. How many like neither?
A bag holds 6 red, 3 green and 2 blue balls. One ball is drawn at random. What is the probability that it is blue?
e: There are 2 favourable balls out of 11, so the probability is 2/11.

q: A bag holds 3 red, 7 green and 2 blue balls. One ball is drawn at random. What is the probability that it is blue?
e: There are 2 favourable balls out of 12, so the probability is 1/6.

q: A bag holds 4 red, 2 green and 3 blue balls. One ball is drawn at random. What is the probability that it is blue?
e: There are 3 favourable balls out of 9, so the probability is 1/3.

q: Two fair dice are thrown. What is the probability that the two numbers add up to 7?
e: There are 36 equally likely outcomes. The favourable ones are (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1): 6 in all. Probability = 1/6.

q: Two fair dice are thrown. What is the probability that the two numbers add up to 4?
e: There are 36 equally likely outcomes. The favourable ones are (1,3), (2,2), (3,1): 3 in all. Probability = 1/12.

q: What is the median of 24, 5, 13, 4, 22?
e: Arrange in order: 4, 5, 13, 22, 24. The middle value is 13.

q: What is the median of 32, 15, 30, 13, 9, 40, 19?
e: Arrange in order: 9, 13, 15, 19, 30, 32, 40. The middle value is 19.

q: What is the range of 7, 14, 22, 19, 21, 19, 19?
e: Range = largest − smallest = 22 − 7 = 15.

q: What is the range of 8, 23, 4, 8, 6, 10, 8?
e: Range = largest − smallest = 23 − 4 = 19.

q: How many diagonals does a polygon with 9 sides have?
12 teams play a league in which every team plays every other team once. How many matches are played?
e: Number of pairs = n(n − 1) ÷ 2 = 12 × 11 ÷ 2 = 66.

q: How many diagonals does a polygon with 6 sides have?
e: Diagonals = n(n − 3) ÷ 2 = 6 × 3 ÷ 2 = 9.

q: Students enrolled in a college: 2020: 200; 2021: 420; 2022: 540; 2023: 600; 2024: 520. In how many of the five years was the figure above the five-year average?
e: Average = 2280 ÷ 5 = 456. The figures above it: 540, 600, 520. That is 3 years.

q: Exports of a firm (Rs million): 2019: 280; 2020: 600; 2021: 320; 2022: 120; 2023: 460. What is the percentage change from 2020 to 2022?
e: Change = 120 − 600 = −480. As a percentage of the 2020 figure: 480 ÷ 600 × 100 = 80% decrease.

q: Visitors to a museum (thousands): 2019: 220; 2020: 240; 2021: 120; 2022: 280; 2023: 420. What is the ratio of the 2020 figure to the 2021 figure in its lowest terms?
e: 240 : 120. Divide both by 120 to get 2 : 1.

q: Visitors to a museum (thousands): 2019: 180; 2020: 360; 2021: 280; 2022: 200; 2023: 160. What is the ratio of the 2020 figure to the 2019 figure in its lowest terms?
e: 360 : 180. Divide both by 180 to get 2 : 1.

q: Visitors to a museum (thousands): 2019: 120; 2020: 580; 2021: 200; 2022: 540; 2023: 380. In which year was the rise over the previous year the greatest?
e: Year-on-year changes: 460, −380, 340, −160. The greatest rise, 460, came in 2020.

q: Exports of a firm (Rs million): 2021: 220; 2022: 160; 2023: 440; 2024: 140; 2025: 500. What is the average for the five years?
e: Total = 1460. Average = 1460 ÷ 5 = 292.

q: Students enrolled in a college: 2022: 280; 2023: 400; 2024: 180; 2025: 560; 2026: 260. What is the percentage change from 2022 to 2025?
e: Change = 560 − 280 = 280. As a percentage of the 2022 figure: 280 ÷ 280 × 100 = 100% increase.

q: Students enrolled in a college: 2022: 260; 2023: 160; 2024: 300; 2025: 480; 2026: 200. In which year was the rise over the previous year the greatest?
e: Year-on-year changes: −100, 140, 180, −280. The greatest rise, 180, came in 2025.

q: Visitors to a museum (thousands): 2022: 440; 2023: 280; 2024: 100; 2025: 220; 2026: 120. In which year was the rise over the previous year the greatest?
e: Year-on-year changes: −160, −180, 120, −100. The greatest rise, 120, came in 2025.

q: Visitors to a museum (thousands): 2020: 360; 2021: 300; 2022: 260; 2023: 420; 2024: 380. In which year was the rise over the previous year the greatest?
e: Year-on-year changes: −60, −40, 160, −40. The greatest rise, 160, came in 2023.

q: What is the next number in the series 6, 11, 18, 27, 38, 51, ...?
e: The terms are squares of 2, 3, 4 ... plus 2. The next term is 66.

q: What is the next number in the series 5, 7, 11, 17, 25, 35, ...?
e: The differences are 2, 4, 6, 8, 10; they grow by 2 each time. Next difference is 12. The next term is 47.

q: What is the next number in the series 6, 13, 27, 55, 111, 223, ...?
e: Each term is double the previous term plus 1. The next term is 447.

q: What is the next number in the series 2, 5, 10, 17, 26, 37, ...?
e: The terms are squares of 1, 2, 3 ... plus 1. The next term is 50.

q: What is the next number in the series 2, 7, 17, 37, 77, 157, ...?
e: Each term is double the previous term plus 3. The next term is 317.

q: What is the next number in the series 0, 7, 26, 63, 124, 215, ...?
e: The terms are cubes of 1, 2, 3 ... minus 1. The next term is 342.

q: What is the next number in the series 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, ...?
e: Each term is 2 times the previous term. The next term is 128.

q: What is the next number in the series 2, 4, 6, 10, 16, 26, ...?
e: Each term is the sum of the two terms before it. The next term is 42.

q: What is the next number in the series 3, 6, 12, 24, 48, 96, ...?
e: Each term is 2 times the previous term. The next term is 192.

q: What is the next number in the series 12, 20, 30, 42, 56, 72, ...?
e: Each term is n(n + 1): 3×4, 4×5 .... The next term is 90.

q: What comes next in the series G5, I6, K7, M8, ...?
e: The letter moves forward 2 places and the number rises by 1. The next term is O9.

q: What comes next in the series D, E, G, J, ...?
e: The gaps between letters grow by one each time (1, 2, 3, 4). The next term is N.

q: What comes next in the series C, D, F, I, ...?
e: The gaps between letters grow by one each time (1, 2, 3, 4). The next term is M.

q: What comes next in the series DW, EV, FU, GT, ...?
e: The first letter moves forward and the second letter moves backward by one place. The next term is HS.

q: What comes next in the series I1, K2, M3, O4, ...?
e: The letter moves forward 2 places and the number rises by 1. The next term is Q5.

q: What comes next in the series G2, J3, M4, P5, ...?
e: The letter moves forward 3 places and the number rises by 1. The next term is S6.

q: A sequence starts with 3. To get each next term you alternately multiply by 3 and subtract 3, starting with the multiplication. What is the 5th term?
e: The terms are 3, 9, 6, 18, 15. The 5th term is 15.

q: A sequence starts with 9. To get each next term you alternately multiply by 2 and subtract 5, starting with the multiplication. What is the 5th term?
e: The terms are 9, 18, 13, 26, 21. The 5th term is 21.

q: A sequence starts with 9. To get each next term you alternately multiply by 3 and subtract 5, starting with the multiplication. What is the 7th term?
e: The terms are 9, 27, 22, 66, 61, 183, 178. The 7th term is 178.
In the first pair the second number is the first multiplied by the next whole number. Apply the same rule to 10: 110.
In the first pair the second number is the first multiplied by the next whole number. Apply the same rule to 9: 90.
In the first pair the second number is the cube of the first. Apply the same rule to 10: 1000.
In the first pair the second number is three times the first plus 1. Apply the same rule to 9: 28.
In the first pair the second number is the first multiplied by the next whole number. Apply the same rule to 10: 110.

q: Which is the odd one out: Mercury, Venus, Moon, Mars?
e: The Moon is a satellite; the others are planets.

q: Which is the odd one out: Lahore, Karachi, Peshawar, Multan?
e: Multan is not a provincial capital.

q: Which is the odd one out: 17, 23, 29, 33?
e: 33 = 3 × 11 is not prime.

q: Which is the odd one out: litre, kilogram, gallon, pint?
e: The kilogram measures mass; the others measure volume.

q: Which is the odd one out: 16, 25, 36, 48?
e: 48 is not a perfect square.

q: Which is the odd one out: Indus, Jhelum, Chenab, Karakoram?
e: Karakoram is a mountain range; the others are rivers.

q: Which is the odd one out: January, March, June, July?
e: June has 30 days; the others have 31.

q: Which is the odd one out: 121, 169, 196, 200?
e: 121, 169 and 196 are the squares of 11, 13 and 14.

q: In a certain code, TIGER is written as WLJHU. How is PLANT written in that code?
e: Each letter is moved 3 places forward in the alphabet. So PLANT becomes SODQW.

q: In a certain code, BRICK is written as EULFN. How is LIGHT written in that code?
e: Each letter is moved 3 places forward in the alphabet. So LIGHT becomes OLJKW.

q: In a certain code, SUGAR is written as RTFZQ. How is PEARL written in that code?
e: Each letter is moved 1 place backward in the alphabet. So PEARL becomes ODZQK.

q: In a certain code, WATER is written as ZDWHU. How is CHAIR written in that code?
e: Each letter is moved 3 places forward in the alphabet. So CHAIR becomes FKDLU.

q: In a certain code, MANGO is written as KYLEM. How is HOUSE written in that code?
e: Each letter is moved 2 places backward in the alphabet. So HOUSE becomes FMSQC.

q: If A = 1, B = 2, C = 3 and so on, and DOG = 26, what is the value of HEN?
e: Add the positions of the letters: 8 + 5 + 14 = 27.

q: In a code, letters are numbered backwards (Z = 1, Y = 2, ... A = 26) and NET is written as 13-22-7. How is OWL written?
e: Each letter becomes 27 minus its normal position. OWL is 12-4-15.

q: If A = 1, B = 2, C = 3 and so on, and RUG = 46, what is the value of OWL?
e: Add the positions of the letters: 15 + 23 + 12 = 50.

q: If A = 1, B = 2, C = 3 and so on, and BAG = 10, what is the value of PEN?
e: Add the positions of the letters: 16 + 5 + 14 = 35.

q: A man walks 9 km north and then 12 km east. How far is he from his starting point?
e: The two legs are at right angles. Distance = √(9² + 12²) = √225 = 15 km.

q: A man walks 11 km north, then 24 km east, then 4 km south. How far is he from his starting point?
e: His net movement is 7 km north and 24 km east. Distance = √(7² + 24²) = 25 km.

q: A man walks 7 km north and then 24 km east. How far is he from his starting point?
e: The two legs are at right angles. Distance = √(7² + 24²) = √625 = 25 km.

q: A man is facing south. He turns 90° to his right, then 90° to his left, and then 135° to his right. Which direction is he facing now?
e: Count right turns as clockwise and left turns as anticlockwise from south. He ends up facing north-west.

q: A man is facing south. He turns 135° to his right, then 135° to his left, and then 90° to his left. Which direction is he facing now?
e: Count right turns as clockwise and left turns as anticlockwise from south. He ends up facing east.

q: A man is facing west. He turns 45° to his right, then 135° to his right, and then 135° to his left. Which direction is he facing now?
e: Count right turns as clockwise and left turns as anticlockwise from west. He ends up facing north-west.

q: A man is facing east. He turns 135° to his right, then 45° to his left, and then 180° to his right. Which direction is he facing now?
e: Count right turns as clockwise and left turns as anticlockwise from east. He ends up facing north.

q: What is the smaller angle between the hour hand and the minute hand of a clock at 9:24?
e: Hour hand: 30 × 9 + 0.5 × 24 = 282°. Minute hand: 6 × 24 = 144°. The smaller angle between them is 138°.

q: What is the smaller angle between the hour hand and the minute hand of a clock at 2:36?
e: Hour hand: 30 × 2 + 0.5 × 36 = 78°. Minute hand: 6 × 36 = 216°. The smaller angle between them is 138°.

q: What is the smaller angle between the hour hand and the minute hand of a clock at 4:50?
e: Hour hand: 30 × 4 + 0.5 × 50 = 145°. Minute hand: 6 × 50 = 300°. The smaller angle between them is 155°.

q: A clock shows 11:50. What time does its image in a mirror appear to show?
e: Subtract the time from 12:00 (think of 11:60). 11:60 − 11:50 = 12:10.

q: A clock shows 6:25. What time does its image in a mirror appear to show?
e: Subtract the time from 12:00 (think of 11:60). 11:60 − 6:25 = 5:35.

q: Today is Saturday. What day of the week will it be 61 days from today?
e: 61 ÷ 7 leaves a remainder of 5. Count 5 day(s) forward from Saturday: Thursday.

q: Today is Thursday. What day of the week will it be 125 days from today?
e: 125 ÷ 7 leaves a remainder of 6. Count 6 day(s) forward from Thursday: Wednesday.

q: 1 January 2029 is a Monday. What day of the week is 1 December 2029?
e: 2029 is not a leap year. From 1 January to 1 December is 334 days, and 334 ÷ 7 leaves remainder 5. Count 5 day(s) forward from Monday: Saturday.

q: 1 January 2027 is a Friday. What day of the week is 1 December 2027?
e: 2027 is not a leap year. From 1 January to 1 December is 334 days, and 334 ÷ 7 leaves remainder 5. Count 5 day(s) forward from Friday: Wednesday.

q: 1 January 2028 is a Saturday. What day of the week is 1 September 2028?
e: 2028 is a leap year. From 1 January to 1 September is 244 days, and 244 ÷ 7 leaves remainder 6. Count 6 day(s) forward from Saturday: Friday.

q: A bus leaves a stop every 52 minutes. A clerk says: "The last bus left 37 minutes ago and the next one leaves at 8:50." At what time is the clerk speaking?
e: The last bus left at 8:50 minus 52 minutes = 7:58. Add 37 minutes: 8:35.

q: A bus leaves a stop every 20 minutes. A clerk says: "The last bus left 7 minutes ago and the next one leaves at 7:30." At what time is the clerk speaking?
e: The last bus left at 7:30 minus 20 minutes = 7:10. Add 7 minutes: 7:17.

q: In a class of 32 students, Omar ranks 10th from the top. What is his rank from the bottom?
e: Rank from the bottom = 32 − 10 + 1 = 23.

q: In a class of 35 students, Omar ranks 8th from the top. What is his rank from the bottom?
e: Rank from the bottom = 35 − 8 + 1 = 28.

q: In a row of students, Hina is 6th from the left end and 16th from the right end. How many students are in the row?
e: Total = 6 + 16 − 1 = 21, because Hina is counted twice.

q: In a queue, Ali is 10th from the front and Bilal is 12th from the back. There are 5 people between them and Ali is ahead of Bilal. How many people are in the queue?
Danish is lighter than Imran. Imran is lighter than Junaid. Danish is heavier than Hamid. Fahad is lighter than Hamid. Who is the second lightest?
e: Putting the clues together, the order from heaviest to lightest is Junaid, Imran, Danish, Hamid, Fahad. So the answer is Hamid.

q: Imran is shorter than Junaid. Junaid is shorter than Fahad. Ejaz is taller than Fahad. Danish is taller than Ejaz. Who is the shortest?
e: Putting the clues together, the order from tallest to shortest is Danish, Ejaz, Fahad, Junaid, Imran. So the answer is Imran.

q: Junaid is younger than Imran. Junaid is older than Hamid. Asad is older than Imran. Ejaz is younger than Hamid. Who is exactly in the middle?
e: Putting the clues together, the order from oldest to youngest is Asad, Imran, Junaid, Hamid, Ejaz. So the answer is Junaid.

q: Ghani is heavier than Hamid. Junaid is lighter than Hamid. Chand is heavier than Danish. Danish is heavier than Ghani. Who is the lightest?
e: Putting the clues together, the order from heaviest to lightest is Chand, Danish, Ghani, Hamid, Junaid. So the answer is Junaid.

q: Ghani is lighter than Ejaz. Chand is heavier than Hamid. Ghani is heavier than Junaid. Junaid is heavier than Chand. Who is the second heaviest?
e: Putting the clues together, the order from heaviest to lightest is Ejaz, Ghani, Junaid, Chand, Hamid. So the answer is Ghani.

q: If the words Infant, Inflate, Infuse, Inform are arranged as in a dictionary, which word comes second?
e: Dictionary order: Infant, Inflate, Inform, Infuse. The second word is Inflate.

q: If the words Translate, Transmit, Transfer, Transit are arranged as in a dictionary, which word comes first?
e: Dictionary order: Transfer, Transit, Translate, Transmit. The first word is Transfer.

q: If the words Station, Status, Static, Statute are arranged as in a dictionary, which word comes first?
e: Dictionary order: Static, Station, Status, Statute. The first word is Static.

q: Pointing to a girl in a photograph, Ahmed said, 'She is the daughter of my paternal grandfather's only son.' How is the girl related to Ahmed?
e: The only son of Ahmed's paternal grandfather is Ahmed's father. His daughter is Ahmed's sister.

q: P is the mother of Q. Q is the sister of R. R is the son of S. How is S related to P?
e: Q and R are children of P. S is the other parent of R, so S is P's husband.

q: X is the father of Y. Y is the brother of Z. Z is the mother of W. How is X related to W?
e: X is the father of Z, and Z is W's mother. So X is W's maternal grandfather.

q: M is the son of N. N is the daughter of O. O is the wife of K. How is M related to K?
e: N is the daughter of O and K. M is N's son, so M is K's grandson.

q: A and B are brothers. C and D are sisters. A's son is D's brother. How is B related to C?
e: A's son is D's brother, so D and her sister C are A's daughters. B is A's brother, so B is C's uncle.

q: Looking at a portrait, a man said, 'I have no brother or sister, but that man's father is my father's son.' Whose portrait is it?
e: With no brothers, 'my father's son' is the speaker himself. So the speaker is the father of the man in the portrait.

q: Tariq is Usman's father. Usman is Wajid's brother. Wajid is Yasir's father. How is Tariq related to Yasir?
e: Tariq is also Wajid's father, and Wajid is Yasir's father. So Tariq is Yasir's grandfather.

q: All roses are flowers. All flowers are plants. Which conclusion must be true?
e: If every rose is a flower and every flower is a plant, every rose is a plant.

q: No fish is a bird. All sparrows are birds. Which conclusion must be true?
e: Sparrows are inside the group of birds, and no bird is a fish.

q: All clerks in an office are graduates. Ali is a clerk in that office. Which conclusion must be true?
e: Ali belongs to a group all of whose members are graduates.

q: Some doctors are writers. No writer is lazy. Which conclusion must be true?
e: The doctors who are writers cannot be lazy. Nothing is known about the other doctors.

q: Every file cleared by Section A carries a stamp. File 7 carries no stamp. Which conclusion must be true?
o: File 7 was cleared by Section A
File 7 was not cleared by Section A
File 7 was cleared by another section
Every stamped file was cleared by Section A
e: If Section A had cleared it, it would carry a stamp. Whether another section cleared it is not known.

q: No manager is a clerk. Some clerks are typists. Which conclusion must be true?
e: The typists who are clerks cannot be managers.

q: All A are B. No B is C. Which conclusion must be true?
e: A lies wholly inside B, and B has nothing in common with C.

q: 'If it rains, the match is cancelled.' Which statement is logically equivalent?
o: If the match is not cancelled, it did not rain
The match is cancelled only when it rains
If the match is cancelled, it rained
If it does not rain, the match is not cancelled
e: 'If P then Q' is equivalent to its contrapositive, 'If not Q then not P'.

q: What is the negation of 'All students passed'?
o: At least one student did not pass
e: To deny "all" you need only one exception.

q: Applicants are shortlisted only if they score at least 70 and have two years of experience. Ali scored 82 and has one year of experience. What follows?
o: Nothing can be said about Ali
Ali is shortlisted because his score is high
e: Both conditions are necessary. He fails the experience condition.

q: 'Students who sleep at least seven hours score higher on average than those who sleep less.' Which conclusion is best supported?
o: Sleep and scores are associated in this group
Every student who sleeps seven hours will score high
e: An average difference shows an association, not a rule for every student.

q: If A is true, then B is true. B is false. What follows?
o: Nothing can be said about A
e: This is denying the consequent (modus tollens): not B, therefore not A.

q: A manager says: 'Sales rose after we changed the logo, so the new logo caused the rise.' What is the weakness of this argument?
o: It repeats its conclusion as a reason
It assumes that what happens after an event is caused by it
It attacks a person instead of an argument
e: This is the "after this, therefore because of this" error.

q: Five friends sit in a row facing north. Danish is at the left end and Ejaz is at the right end. Asad is in the middle. Bilal is immediately to the right of Asad. Where does Chand sit?
e: From the left: Danish, Chand, Asad, Bilal, Ejaz.

q: Five books P, Q, R, S and T are in a pile. Q is above R but below P. S is at the bottom. T is directly above S. Which book is in the middle of the pile?
e: From the top: P, Q, R, T, S. The third book is R.

q: Five talks (Maths, History, Art, Physics, Law) are given from Monday to Friday, one a day. Maths is on Monday. History is on Wednesday. Physics is on the day after Art. Which talk is on Friday?
e: Art and Physics need two days in a row, which leaves only Thursday and Friday. So Law is on Tuesday and Physics is on Friday.

q: Three boxes are labelled 'Apples', 'Oranges' and 'Mixed', and every label is wrong. A fruit taken from the box labelled 'Mixed' is an apple. What does the box labelled 'Oranges' contain?
e: The box labelled 'Mixed' must hold apples only. The box labelled 'Oranges' cannot hold oranges, and apples are taken, so it holds mixed fruit.

q: A, B, C, D and E sit in a row. A and B sit at the two ends. C sits next to A. D does not sit next to B. Who sits next to B?
e: The row is A, C, D, E, B (or its mirror image). E is next to B.

q: If the day before yesterday was Thursday, what day will the day after tomorrow be?
e: Today is Saturday. The day after tomorrow is Monday.

q: What is the value of x? Statement I: x + 5 = 12. Statement II: x is a positive number.
o: Even both statements together are not sufficient
e: Statement I gives x = 7. Statement II alone gives no value.

q: What is the area of a rectangle? Statement I: Its length is 12 cm. Statement II: Its perimeter is 40 cm.
o: Even both statements together are not sufficient
e: Together: width = 20 − 12 = 8 cm, so the area is 96 cm². Neither statement is enough alone.

q: What is the integer n? Statement I: n lies between 20 and 30. Statement II: n is a multiple of 9.
o: Even both statements together are not sufficient
e: The only multiple of 9 between 20 and 30 is 27.

q: Which is larger, a or b? Statement I: a − b = 3. Statement II: a + b = 10.
o: Even both statements together are not sufficient
e: A positive difference a − b shows that a is larger.

q: What is the value of y? Statement I: y² = 49. Statement II: y is negative.
o: Even both statements together are not sufficient
e: Statement I gives 7 or −7. Statement II picks −7.

q: How many Surahs are there in the Holy Quran?
e: The Quran has 114 Surahs arranged in 30 Paras (Juz).

q: The Quran is divided into how many Manzils (stages for weekly recitation)?
e: Seven Manzils allow the Quran to be completed in a week.

q: The first revelation came to the Holy Prophet (PBUH) in which cave?
e: The first five verses of Surah Al-Alaq were revealed in Cave Hira in 610 CE.

q: The first revealed verses belong to which Surah?
e: "Iqra" (Read) opens Surah Al-Alaq, the first revelation.

q: Which is the longest Surah of the Quran?
e: Al-Baqarah has 286 verses and 40 Rukus.

q: Which is the shortest Surah of the Quran?
e: Al-Kawthar has only three verses.

q: Which Surah does not begin with Bismillah?
e: Surah At-Tawbah (Bara'ah), the ninth Surah, has no Bismillah at its start.

q: In which Surah does Bismillah appear twice?
e: It opens the Surah and appears again in the letter of Hazrat Sulaiman (27:30).

q: Which Surah is called the "heart of the Quran"?
e: A well-known Hadith describes Surah Yaseen as the heart of the Quran.

q: Which Surah is known as "Aroos-ul-Quran" (the bride of the Quran)?
e: Surah Ar-Rahman carries this title.

q: "Umm-ul-Kitab" (Mother of the Book) is a name of which Surah?
e: Al-Fatihah is also called As-Sab'ul-Mathani and Ash-Shifa.

q: Reciting which Surah is said to equal one-third of the Quran?
e: Al-Ikhlas states pure Tawhid and is described as one-third of the Quran.
